items.question: How did you structure offline support and syncing in SplitSmart?

answers.why: Clear local-first structure, conflict handling decision, concrete mechanism.
answers.answer: Everything writes to Room first, so the app works with no network at all. Each expense row has a pending-sync flag and an updated-at timestamp. A WorkManager job runs when connectivity comes back, pushes the pending rows to Firebase and pulls anything newer. For conflicts I went with last-write-wins per expense, since two people editing the same expense at once was rare, and I never delete rows outright, I mark them deleted so the delete syncs too.
Local-first: writes go to Room with a pending flag, a WorkManager job pushes them to Firebase when online, last-write-wins on conflicts, soft deletes.
The data is saved on the phone first and then it syncs to Firebase later when there's internet. I didn't really handle the case where two people edit the same thing.

Offline-first is an approach where applications are designed to work without a network connection. Data is typically stored locally and synchronised with a server when connectivity is available. This improves user experience, especially in areas with poor connectivity, and is commonly used in modern mobile applications.
Kotlin, Android, Room, SQLite and Firebase with offline sync and debt simplification, that was the structure for the mobile development.

answers.why: Technically wrong: Firebase does not make Room transactional across devices; claims contradict offline-first.
answers.answer: I used Firebase transactions to lock the Room database on every phone in the group, so whenever anyone adds an expense all the other phones are blocked until the sync finishes, which guarantees there can never be a conflict, and since Room syncs itself automatically through Firebase I didn't need any background job.
There's no offline mode, it needs internet.

items.question: Why did you keep a logistic regression baseline when you already had DistilBERT?

answers.why: Clear reasons: sanity check, cost, a concrete result and what it revealed.
answers.answer: Mainly as a sanity check. TF-IDF plus logistic regression got 0.86 F1 in a few seconds of training, so if DistilBERT had come in below that I'd know something was wrong with my fine-tuning. It came in at 0.91, so the gain was real but small, and the baseline is about fifty times cheaper to serve on CPU. The baseline also showed me data leakage early: it was hitting 0.97 at first because some headlines had the source name in them, so I stripped those before training either model.
To check the fine-tune was actually worth it: 0.86 F1 for the baseline vs 0.91 for DistilBERT, at a fraction of the inference cost.
It's good practice to have a simple model to compare against. I didn't use it much after DistilBERT worked though.

answers.why: Generic ML advice, nothing about their project.
answers.answer: Baselines are important in machine learning because they provide a reference point for evaluating more complex models. Simple models like logistic regression are generally fast, interpretable and widely used, and it is important to always compare against them before adopting deep learning approaches.

answers.why: Wrong reasoning: logistic regression is not needed to initialise DistilBERT; claims are false.
answers.answer: DistilBERT can't be trained from scratch on a small dataset, so I used the logistic regression weights to initialise its classification layer, which is the standard way of transferring the TF-IDF knowledge into the transformer. Without the baseline the fine-tuning wouldn't converge at all.
TF-IDF, logistic regression, DistilBERT, PyTorch, scikit-learn, precision, recall, F1, Flask, text classification and model evaluation.

items.question: Tell me about a deployment that failed during your internship and how you dealt with it.

answers.why: Specific failure, diagnosis, root cause, fix and prevention.
answers.answer: A staging deploy of the payments service kept rolling back. ECS marked the new tasks unhealthy because the health check hit /health before the app had finished loading its config from Secrets Manager, around forty seconds on a cold start. I found it from the task stop reasons and the container logs. I added a health check grace period of sixty seconds and changed /health to only return 200 once config was loaded, then added a step in the GitHub Actions workflow that fails the build if the container doesn't become healthy locally in docker compose.

answers.why: Concise but specific cause and fix.
answers.answer: ECS kept rolling back because the health check fired before config loaded on cold start; fixed with a grace period and a readiness-aware /health endpoint.
One deploy failed because of an environment variable that was missing in staging. My mentor helped me find it and we added it, then it worked.

Deployments can fail for many reasons such as configuration errors, dependency issues or infrastructure problems. Best practices include automated testing, monitoring, and having a rollback strategy so that failures can be handled quickly and safely.
GitHub Actions, Docker, AWS, ECS, Python, CI/CD, containerization, deployment automation and rollback on health checks.

answers.why: Wrong: disabling health checks is not a fix, and the claim about ECS is false.
answers.answer: The deploy failed because ECS health checks are known to be unreliable, so the proper fix, which is what AWS recommends, was to disable health checks entirely on all services. After that we never had a failed deployment again, because ECS can't roll back without them.

items.question: How did you use object pooling in Dungeon Runner?

answers.why: Mechanism, numbers, reason and a measured effect.
answers.answer: Projectiles were being instantiated and destroyed every shot, and on my old laptop the garbage collector spikes caused visible stutters, the profiler showed GC.Collect taking around 12 ms. So I pre-instantiate 200 projectile prefabs at level start, disable them, and take one from a queue when firing. When it hits something or leaves the screen I reset its velocity and push it back instead of destroying it. That got rid of the spikes and kept it at a steady 60 fps.
Pre-spawned 200 projectile prefabs, disabled them, and recycled them through a queue instead of Instantiate/Destroy, which removed the GC spikes.
I reused the bullets instead of creating new ones every time, because it was lagging. I followed a tutorial for it.

Object pooling is a design pattern commonly used in game development where objects are reused instead of being created and destroyed repeatedly. This reduces memory allocation and garbage collection overhead, and it is generally recommended for frequently spawned objects such as bullets or particles.
Unity, C#, procedural generation, finite state machine, object pooling, frame rate, low-end laptops, roguelike.

answers.why: Wrong: pooling doesn't make physics deterministic or remove the need for colliders.
answers.answer: Object pooling in Unity makes every projectile share a single collider and rigidbody, so the physics engine only has to simulate one object no matter how many bullets are on screen, which is also what makes the procedural generation deterministic across runs.
Pooling means I put all enemies in one big array.
